body_markdown:
At several oncology conferences this year, one theme emerged consistently: biomarkers have evolved from valuable scientific tools into indispensable strategic assets in oncology development. Biomarker strategies influence decisions across development, helping biopharma companies reduce risk, improve trial efficiency, and accelerate precision medicine. As oncology science advances, therapeutic approaches are becoming increasingly complex. Cell and gene therapies, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), and immunotherapies all require a deeper understanding of disease biology and patient response. In this environment, biomarkers are helping guide target selection, inform go/no-go decisions, optimize clinical development strategies, and shape regulatory pathways.


Join our conversation with Taylor Jensen, PhD, vice president and head of oncology science at Labcorp, for a discussion on the growing strategic role of biomarkers and how biomarker strategies are reshaping oncology research and development.


Image


## Why have biomarkers become such a critical part of oncology drug development?


Historically, biomarkers were often incorporated later in development to support patient selection. Drug developers are now integrating biomarker strategies earlier in development to influence critical development decisions and improve the likelihood of clinical success.


Predictive, prognostic, and pharmacodynamic biomarkers can help answer key questions throughout development:


- ***Which patients are most likely to respond?***
- ***How can efficacy be measured earlier?***
- ***What mechanisms drive resistance?***


As therapeutic modalities become more complex, the need for sophisticated diagnostic approaches increases. Developers are increasingly utilizing platforms and biomarker strategies tailored to the unique mechanisms of these emerging treatments.


## How can biomarkers help reduce development risk?


Drug development is an inherently high-risk endeavor. Biomarker integration can help drug developers proactively identify and manage risk throughout clinical development, and selecting the most appropriate assay platform is critical. Whether utilizing PCR, IHC, NGS, or digital pathology technologies, developers must balance analytical performance, scalability, regulatory considerations, and clinical utility. The wrong platform choice can delay development and complicate diagnostic commercialization.


As sponsors navigate an increasingly complex global regulatory environment, advances in biomarker science are simultaneously reshaping the future of oncology drug development. Molecular residual disease (MRD) provides a compelling example of this progress. Its acceptance as an early endpoint in multiple myeloma trials demonstrates how well-validated biomarkers can potentially accelerate development timelines by providing earlier indicators of clinical benefit.


## How are biomarker strategies improving patient identification and trial enrollment?


Patient identification remains one of the most significant challenges in oncology clinical trials. Increasingly, organizations are moving beyond single-marker testing toward more comprehensive approaches that integrate molecular and pathological data. Multi-omic and multi-modal profiling help sponsors better understand tumor biology and patient heterogeneity. Technologies such as epigenomic profiling, liquid biopsy testing, and digital pathology help identify patients most likely to benefit from investigational therapies.


> **"The future isn't about relying on one biomarker to guide decisions. It's about integrating multiple layers of biological information to create a more complete picture of disease and ultimately connect the right patients with the right therapies."**
>
>
> *– Taylor Jensen, VP, Head of Science, Oncology*


## What are sponsors looking for from biomarker and diagnostics partners?


As biomarker programs grow more sophisticated, sponsors are seeking lab partners that can provide more than individual testing services. They are looking for organizations capable of supporting biomarker strategies throughout development.


Perhaps most importantly, sponsors need confidence that their partners can evolve alongside emerging biomarker modalities and diagnostic platforms. The ability to integrate new technologies while maintaining operational consistency is becoming a key differentiator.


> " ***Scientific innovation alone isn't enough. Sponsors need partners who can generate consistent, high-quality data across studies, regions, and platforms. That continuity becomes critical when you're making development decisions that may impact an entire program** ."*
>
>
> *– Taylor Jensen, VP, Head of Science, Oncology*


## What does the future of biomarker-driven oncology development look like?


The future of oncology development will likely be defined by even broader use of biomarker-driven approaches. Emerging technologies, such as liquid biopsy, MRD monitoring, and multi-cancer early detection biomarkers (MCED), have the potential to transform how clinical trials are designed and how patients receive care.


To support these advances, integrated laboratory partners can help bring together genomic testing, liquid biopsy, pathology, and global laboratory capabilities into a streamlined, standardized framework. By connecting clinical, diagnostic, and operational data, these solutions support better decisions and greater efficiency.


As oncology science continues to evolve, biomarkers are expected to remain central to reducing uncertainty, improving trial efficiency, and advancing precision medicine.
